puzzles.funFact: The Serengeti's annual migration is the largest land mammal migration on Earth — about 8 million hooves moving in a continuous loop. From the air, the herds form rivers stretching to the horizon.
puzzles.teaser: Every year, millions of animals move in a vast arc across the plain, following rain. No one leads. No one needs to.

puzzles.imageDescription: A massive flat-topped mountain rises 1,085 meters above a beautiful coastal city, its sandstone plateau extending nearly 3 km from end to end like a perfect natural table. White cottony clouds often spill over the rim creating the famous 'tablecloth' effect. Below, a colorful city stretches to the deep blue Atlantic Ocean, with white sand beaches and dramatic peninsulas visible. A cable car ascends the cliff face.
clues: On certain days a thick blanket of cloud spills over its flat summit — locals call it the 'tablecloth' and have a folk legend about a smoking contest with the devil to explain it.
Its summit plateau is one of the world's most ancient surfaces — about 6 times older than the Himalayas.
Over 2,200 plant species grow on its slopes — more than the entire United Kingdom — and many exist nowhere else.
It rises behind a city at the southwestern tip of Africa, near the Cape of Good Hope.
Table Mountain looms over Cape Town, South Africa.
puzzles.funFact: Table Mountain has the most-photographed peak in Africa — and its 'tablecloth' clouds form because moist sea breezes hit the cool flat plateau and condense on contact, only to evaporate as they spill over the warmer leeward side.
puzzles.teaser: On certain days a cloud settles over the summit and refuses to leave. Locals have a name for it. The mountain ignores them.

puzzles.imageDescription: An extinct volcano with a flat snow-capped summit rises 5,895 meters above golden African savanna grasslands. The mountain's distinctive silhouette dominates the horizon, with multiple ecological zones visible from low scrubland through forest, moorland, alpine desert, and finally a glaciated dome. Acacia trees, elephants, and giraffes graze in the foreground, and pure white snow on a peak so close to the equator creates a striking visual contrast.
clues: It is the highest free-standing mountain in the world — meaning it rises from a flat plain rather than from a mountain range.
Its glacial ice cap on the equator is one of the most rapidly retreating glaciers on Earth — likely to disappear entirely by the 2040s.
Around 35,000 people attempt the summit every year, and roughly 10 will die in the attempt.
It towers above the plains of northeastern Tanzania, near the Kenyan border.
Mount Kilimanjaro is in northeastern Tanzania.
puzzles.funFact: Despite sitting just 3 degrees south of the equator, Kilimanjaro has had a permanent ice cap for 11,700 years. Hemingway's famous 1936 short story 'The Snows of Kilimanjaro' contains a now-poignant warning about its melting.
puzzles.teaser: It stands alone on a flat plain, higher than everything around it. From the savannah below, you can see the ice at its peak. Scientists say it won't be there much longer.

puzzles.imageDescription: Eleven extraordinary churches carved entirely from solid bedrock, sunk into deep trenches below ground level. The most famous, shaped like a Greek cross, has been chiseled directly into the red volcanic stone with sharp precision. Worshippers in white shawls move through narrow stone passageways and tunnels connecting the underground sanctuaries. Sacred crosses, rock-cut interiors, and centuries-old wall paintings fill the dim spaces.
clues: Eleven medieval churches here weren't built — they were excavated downward from solid rock, leaving the buildings sunken into the earth.
Constructed in the 12th and 13th centuries to create a 'New Jerusalem' for Ethiopian Christians who could no longer reach the Holy Land.
Some of the churches are connected by tunnels representing the journey through life, death, and resurrection.
It sits at 2,500 meters elevation in the highlands of northern Ethiopia.
The rock-hewn churches of Lalibela are in northern Ethiopia.
puzzles.funFact: Local Ethiopian tradition says angels helped build Lalibela's churches at night while human workers slept — a story possibly explaining how 11 multi-story churches could be carved entirely by hand in just 24 years.
puzzles.teaser: They carved eleven churches downward from solid rock — so that God could look down on them from above.

photo.description: person in white dress in front of pink building

puzzles.imageDescription: Thousands of ancient brick and stucco temples, pagodas, and stupas of varying sizes spread across a vast misty plain at sunrise, their distinctive bell-shaped tops piercing low-lying fog. Hot-air balloons drift silently overhead, casting long shadows on the architectural marvels below. The temples come in every shade of red brick, ochre, and weathered white, with the most prominent rising 60 meters or more above lush plains and meandering river bends.
clues: Over 2,200 ancient temples and pagodas — out of an original 10,000 — still stand on this 100 sq km plain after a millennium.
Most were built in just 250 years between the 11th and 13th centuries by a powerful Buddhist kingdom.
A devastating 2016 earthquake damaged hundreds of temples; rebuilding continues to this day.
It sits along the Irrawaddy River in central Myanmar.
Bagan's temple plain stretches across central Myanmar.
puzzles.funFact: Marco Polo allegedly visited Bagan in the 1280s and called it 'one of the finest sights in the world'. Some scholars dispute he actually went there — but the description has stuck.
puzzles.teaser: An empire built thousands of temples across a valley floor and then vanished. The temples didn't.

puzzles.imageDescription: A massive stepped pyramid of pale gray limestone with a small temple at its summit dominates a wide grassy plaza. Carved serpent heads flank the central staircase, and intricate stone carvings cover the temple walls. Surrounding the pyramid are other ruins including a temple of warriors with rows of carved columns, a great ball court, and a circular astronomical observatory. The site is set in dense Yucatan jungle under tropical sun.
clues: Twice a year — on the spring and autumn equinoxes — sunlight on its main pyramid creates the illusion of a serpent slithering down its staircase.
Clap your hands at the foot of its main pyramid and the echo returns sounding like the call of a sacred quetzal bird — by design.
It was a major regional capital of the Maya civilization for centuries before being mysteriously abandoned around 1200 AD.
It lies in Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula, surrounded by dense jungle and natural sinkholes called cenotes.
Chichen Itza is in Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula.
puzzles.funFact: Chichen Itza's main pyramid, El Castillo, has 365 steps total — one for each day of the solar year. Climbing it is now banned to protect the structure, after a tourist died falling from it in 2006.
puzzles.teaser: On two days a year, the sun draws a serpent down its staircase. The Maya built that. With shadows.

puzzles.imageDescription: Ancient Maya stone temples and ruins perch atop dramatic limestone cliffs above a brilliant turquoise Caribbean Sea. The light gray weathered stones contrast with the impossibly blue water and white sand beach far below. Iguanas sun themselves on the warm stones while the ruined fortifications, watch towers, and ceremonial buildings frame views of the ocean stretching to the horizon.
clues: It is the only major Maya site built directly on the coast — a sea-facing fortress with an actual beach below the temples.
Once a major trade port, it was inhabited until shortly after the Spanish arrived in the early 1500s.
Its name in Maya means 'wall' — for the impressive stone fortifications that protected it on three sides.
It overlooks the Caribbean Sea on Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula, just south of Cancun.
Tulum's clifftop ruins overlook Mexico's Caribbean coast.
puzzles.funFact: Tulum had no single ruler — it was governed by a council of priests, an unusual arrangement among Maya cities. The walls protecting it on three sides date from the 13th century, when raids and conflicts intensified.
puzzles.teaser: Priests governed here, not kings. They built at the edge of a cliff and always kept the sea in sight.

puzzles.imageDescription: An otherworldly desert landscape of red and orange sand and rock formations stretches under deep blue sky, with snow-capped Andean peaks rising in the distance. Massive geysers erupt from the high-altitude plateau, and salt flats reflect the surrounding mountains. Stargazers flock to its dark skies. Strange rock formations, lagoons of brilliant turquoise and red, and pink flamingos wading in salt lakes complete a Mars-like vista.
clues: Some weather stations here have never recorded rainfall — making it the driest non-polar place on Earth.
Astronomers from around the world come here for some of the clearest, darkest skies on the planet — over 300 cloudless nights per year.
Its conditions are so similar to Mars that NASA tests rovers and life-detection equipment here.
It stretches for 1,000 km along the Pacific coast of northern Chile.
The Atacama Desert lies in northern Chile.
puzzles.funFact: Some Atacama riverbeds haven't seen water for hundreds of years. After rare rainfall events, dormant flowers spring up overnight in vast carpets — a phenomenon called 'desierto florido' (the flowering desert).
puzzles.teaser: Almost no rain falls here — sometimes not for years. But when it does, the desert blooms overnight.

puzzles.imageDescription: A massive blue-white glacier stretches 5 km across, terminating in a 70-meter tall jagged ice cliff that plunges into a milky blue lake. Cracks in the ice glow electric blue against the white, and chunks of ice regularly calve into the water with thundering crashes. Wooden viewing platforms allow visitors to watch from a safe distance, with the surrounding Andean mountains and forested shores framing the spectacular scene.
clues: Unlike most glaciers, this one is not retreating — it advances about 2 meters per day, calving icebergs into the lake at the same rate.
Every few years it advances enough to seal off an arm of a glacial lake — pressure builds, and eventually the ice dam dramatically collapses.
It is one of only three glaciers in Patagonia that's stable, despite global warming trends.
It lies in southern Argentina's Los Glaciares National Park, near the town of El Calafate.
Perito Moreno Glacier is in Argentine Patagonia.
puzzles.funFact: The thunderous crashes of ice falling from Perito Moreno's wall happen so frequently that visitors typically witness multiple calving events during a single visit. The largest collapses send waves across the lake.
puzzles.teaser: Every other glacier is retreating. This one keeps advancing — until it collapses into the lake below. Then starts again. It has been doing this for centuries.

puzzles.imageDescription: An ancient stone pedestrian bridge spans a wide river with thirty Baroque statues lining its parapets like a religious procession. The dark blackened stone bridge is flanked by tall medieval gate towers at each end. A historic skyline of red-tiled rooftops, towering Gothic cathedral spires, and a hilltop castle complex rises beyond. Street musicians, artists, and locals walk across the cobbled bridge surface.
clues: Construction began on July 9, 1357, at exactly 5:31 AM — a palindromic moment chosen by an emperor obsessed with numerology.
Tradition says rubbing one of its bronze plaques will guarantee your return to the city — and most plaques shine from millions of touches.
It was the only bridge crossing its river for nearly 500 years, until 1841.
It connects the Old Town and Castle districts of a city sometimes called 'the City of a Hundred Spires'.
Charles Bridge crosses the Vltava River in Prague.
puzzles.funFact: When the Charles Bridge was built, mortar was reinforced with eggs — 50,000 of them, ordered from villages all over Bohemia. Some villages didn't understand the request and arrived with hard-boiled eggs.
puzzles.teaser: Touch the right bronze plaque and you are guaranteed to return. The plaque shines from a million hands that believed it.

puzzles.imageDescription: Dramatic jagged granite peaks rise straight from the deep blue sea, with traditional red-painted wooden fishermen's cabins on stilts dotting the rocky shores. White sandy beaches with turquoise water create a surreal Caribbean-meets-Arctic vibe. The midnight sun illuminates the entire archipelago in summer, while in winter, the northern lights dance overhead. Snow-capped mountains, deep fjords, and quaint fishing villages complete the postcard-perfect scene.
clues: Despite sitting above the Arctic Circle, the warm Gulf Stream keeps the harbors here ice-free year-round.
Its dried cod has been exported to Italy and Portugal for over 1,000 years — and remains a staple of Mediterranean cuisine.
From late May to mid-July, the sun never sets here — and from December to early January, it never rises.
It's an archipelago off the northwestern coast of Norway, deep above the Arctic Circle.
The Lofoten Islands rise from Norway's Arctic coast.
puzzles.funFact: The traditional red color of Lofoten's fishing cabins (called 'rorbuer') comes from a paint historically made from cod liver oil, ochre, and animal blood. Cheap to produce and water-resistant, it became the signature look of Norway's coast.
puzzles.teaser: Above the Arctic Circle, the Gulf Stream keeps the harbour ice-free. In winter, the northern lights. In summer, no night.

puzzles.imageDescription: Cobblestone streets wind uphill past white limestone buildings with traditional Parisian balconies and green shutters. Artists with easels dot the squares, while the iconic white domes of Sacré-Cœur Basilica gleam against the sky. Vintage streetlamps line the narrow alleys, and red windmill blades are visible atop a historic cabaret building.
clues: Around 300 portrait artists still work the Place du Tertre here every day — a tradition unbroken since the 1850s.
Picasso, Van Gogh, Toulouse-Lautrec, and Renoir all lived and worked on the same hill at different times in the late 1800s.
The white basilica at its summit was built as penance for the Franco-Prussian War and completed in 1914.
Its hill is the highest natural point in a famous European capital, topped by a gleaming white basilica.
Montmartre is the artistic hill of Paris.
puzzles.funFact: Montmartre maintains its own working vineyard — about 500 bottles per year. The wine is auctioned for charity, but most locals will tell you it tastes mediocre. It's the symbolism that matters.
puzzles.teaser: Artists came here because they couldn't afford the city below. What they made here changed the city — and everywhere else.

puzzles.imageDescription: Three towering granite spires of dark gray stone rise impossibly straight up from a high plateau, surrounded by glaciers, turquoise lakes, and golden grasslands. The peaks seem to scrape the sky at over 2,500 meters, with their distinct vertical formations created by erosion. Glacial lakes reflect the dramatic mountains while guanacos and condors inhabit the rugged Patagonian wilderness.
clues: Three perfectly vertical granite towers rise like fangs from a barren plateau — they're the result of 12 million years of erosion exposing solid magma chambers.
Wind speeds here regularly exceed 100 mph — strong enough to blow over fully grown adults and rip tents from the ground.
It is the southernmost piece of mainland South America, just 1,800 km from Antarctica.
It sits at the southern tip of Chilean Patagonia, in a region of glaciers and fjords.
Torres del Paine rises from Chilean Patagonia.
puzzles.funFact: The 'Paine' in the name comes from an indigenous Tehuelche word for 'blue' — referring to the deep blue color of the glacial lakes that surround the towers, not the rocks themselves.
puzzles.teaser: The wind here is strong enough to knock you off your feet. The rock above doesn't notice.

puzzles.imageDescription: Hundreds of impossibly tall and slender quartz-sandstone pillars rise straight up from misty subtropical forest valleys, their tops crowned with pine trees and ferns. The columns reach heights over 200 meters with sheer vertical sides, often emerging from clouds and fog at lower elevations. Wooden viewing platforms and a glass bridge stretch between some of the formations, and the surreal landscape inspired the floating mountains in James Cameron's 'Avatar'.
clues: More than 3,000 vertical sandstone pillars rise from this forest — formed by 380 million years of erosion in soft surrounding rock.
James Cameron used these spires as direct visual inspiration for the floating Hallelujah Mountains in 'Avatar' (2009).
A glass-bottom skywalk bridge here, suspended 300 meters above a canyon, is one of the world's highest.
It lies in northwestern Hunan Province in central China.
Zhangjiajie's stone pillars rise in central China.
puzzles.funFact: After 'Avatar' premiered in 2010, China renamed one of the most photogenic pillars 'Avatar Hallelujah Mountain' — a controversial decision that some felt was too commercial for a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
puzzles.teaser: Stone pillars disappear into cloud so high you cannot see their tops. A filmmaker came and said: this is what another world looks like.

puzzles.imageDescription: A surreal landscape featuring bizarre umbrella-shaped Dragon's Blood Trees with thick trunks and flat parasol-like canopies dotting white sandy beaches. The trees have distinctive red resin bleeding from their bark, set against turquoise waters and dramatic limestone cliffs. Pink and white desert roses bloom among the alien-looking vegetation under a bright blue sky.
clues: About a third of its 825 plant species exist nowhere else on Earth — the result of 18 million years of isolation.
Its iconic Dragon's Blood Trees produce a deep red resin that ancient civilizations used as paint, medicine, and dye.
Locals speak Soqotri, an unwritten language with no known relatives — possibly the oldest surviving Semitic tongue.
It lies in the Arabian Sea, far closer to Somalia than to its parent country, Yemen.
Socotra Island belongs to Yemen, in the Arabian Sea.
puzzles.funFact: Socotra is so isolated and otherworldly that biologists call it the 'Galápagos of the Indian Ocean'. About 90% of its reptiles, 95% of its land snails, and 37% of its plants are found nowhere else.
puzzles.teaser: Millions of years of isolation produced a landscape unlike anything else on Earth. The plants here exist in no other country. They look like nothing you have seen before.

puzzles.imageDescription: An enormous flat-topped tabletop mountain with sheer vertical cliff walls rises 2,800 meters above dense tropical rainforest, its summit perpetually shrouded in swirling cloud. The plateau is a unique world with bizarre rock formations, alien-looking carnivorous plants, and constant rainfall. Waterfalls cascade down the 400-meter cliffs in long ribbons, with the rainforest below stretching to a misty horizon.
clues: Its perfectly flat summit was the inspiration for Sir Arthur Conan Doyle's novel 'The Lost World' — and rumors of dinosaurs surviving on top.
The mountain's 31 sq km plateau is so old (around 2 billion years) that it predates almost every form of complex life on Earth.
The summit lies in three countries simultaneously — at the corner where Venezuela, Brazil, and Guyana meet.
It rises from the tropical forests where Venezuela borders Brazil and Guyana.
Mount Roraima is a tepui in southeastern Venezuela.
puzzles.funFact: Mount Roraima's flat top has unique frog and plant species that exist nowhere else — they evolved in isolation atop the plateau, completely cut off from the world below by 400-meter sheer cliffs.
puzzles.teaser: A flat-topped mountain so ancient it predates complex life. Sir Arthur Conan Doyle imagined dinosaurs still lived up there.

photo.description: a man standing next to a boat on a lake

puzzles.imageDescription: Dazzling white calcite terraces cascade down a hillside in a series of shallow pools filled with brilliant turquoise mineral water. The pure white travertine formations look almost like snow or frozen waterfalls, with each pool catching the sunlight in different hues of blue. Visitors walk barefoot across the warm stone, and the ruins of an ancient Greco-Roman city are visible at the top of the white slopes.
clues: Its name in Turkish means 'cotton castle' — for the brilliant white terraces that look like a cascade of fluffy cotton.
The terraces are formed by mineral-rich thermal springs flowing over them, depositing calcium carbonate that hardens into travertine.
An ancient Greco-Roman city called Hierapolis was built atop these springs in the 2nd century BC, with thermal baths still usable today.
It lies in southwestern Turkey, near the city of Denizli.
Pamukkale is in southwestern Turkey.
puzzles.funFact: After decades of damage from tourists trampling the terraces, Turkey banned shoes on Pamukkale in 1997. Visitors now walk barefoot — and damaged sections are slowly self-repairing as new mineral deposits cover the worn footprints.
puzzles.teaser: Hot mineral water has been pouring down white limestone for thousands of years. Civilisations have been coming to bathe here since before Rome arrived.

puzzles.imageDescription: A dirt road runs straight through a row of massive ancient baobab trees, their bulbous trunks stretching upward like giant root vegetables to thin twisted branches at the top. The trees stand 30 meters tall with smooth gray-brown bark, silhouetted dramatically against an orange-purple sunset sky. The flat red-earth landscape stretches to the horizon, with no other significant vegetation interrupting the surreal scene.
clues: These massive trees can store up to 120,000 liters of water in their bulbous trunks — surviving years of drought.
Local Malagasy legend says the trees were planted upside down by an angry god, so their roots reach toward the sky.
These particular specimens are estimated to be 2,800 years old — older than Roman civilization.
It runs along a dirt road in western Madagascar, between Morondava and Belon'i Tsiribihina.
The Avenue of the Baobabs is in western Madagascar.
puzzles.funFact: Madagascar has six of the world's nine baobab species — and they exist nowhere else. The Avenue's trees are the survivors of a once-vast forest that was cleared for rice paddies; only the giants were left standing.
puzzles.teaser: The locals say God planted them upside down. Their roots reach for the sky. Their trunks hold enough water to survive years of drought.

puzzles.imageDescription: An underground cathedral carved entirely from salt, with chandeliers crafted from translucent salt crystals casting warm yellow light over an elaborate carved altar. Salt-sculpted floor tiles, stairs, sculptures, and reliefs cover every surface in shades of white and gray. Lower levels reveal underground lakes that reflect the carvings perfectly, and chapels with biblical scenes are sculpted entirely from rock salt.
clues: Miners working here for over 700 years carved entire chapels, chandeliers, and sculptures from the rock salt — including a complete underground cathedral.
The St. Kinga Chapel inside has chandeliers made of pure salt crystals — when illuminated, they glow as if from within.
The mine descends 327 meters across nine levels — though tourists only see a fraction of its 287 km of tunnels.
It lies just outside the city of Krakow in southern Poland.
The Wieliczka Salt Mine is in southern Poland.
puzzles.funFact: The salt mine's air is so pure (and laced with healthful microparticles) that respiratory patients are sent down 130 meters underground for therapy — a treatment used since 1839.
puzzles.teaser: Seven hundred years of miners carved chapels, sculptures, and chandeliers — all from salt — three hundred metres underground.

photo.description: A tunnel with a train track going through it

puzzles.imageDescription: Massive vertical sandstone pillars rise dramatically from a flat plain, with ancient stone monasteries perched precariously on top of several of the towering rock formations. Each monastery features red-tiled roofs and stone walls that seem to grow directly from the cliff tops. Mist often shrouds the bases of the pillars, making the monasteries appear to float in mid-air. The contrast between the soaring rocks and tiny human structures is breathtaking.
clues: Six Eastern Orthodox monasteries perch atop colossal natural rock pillars — historically reachable only by rope ladder or basket winch.
The first hermits arrived in the 9th century, climbing the rocks to escape persecution and find solitude.
The pillars themselves were formed about 60 million years ago when a primordial sea retreated, leaving sandstone outcrops.
It lies in central Greece, near the town of Kalambaka.
Meteora is in central Greece.
puzzles.funFact: Until the 20th century, monks in Meteora were hauled up to their cliff-top homes in nets attached to ropes — and the ropes were only replaced 'when the Lord lets them break'. They were eventually replaced more often after several deaths.
puzzles.teaser: Monks climbed sheer rock pillars to escape the world. Then they built monasteries on top and invited the world up to visit.

puzzles.imageDescription: A vast flat square cliff plateau juts out 604 meters above a glassy fjord, with the deep blue water of the narrow fjord stretching far below. Hikers stand on the edge of the dramatic 'pulpit-shaped' cliff, dwarfed by the immense scale. Steep mountain walls rise on either side of the fjord, often shrouded in mist. The plateau itself is about 25 by 25 meters of nearly perfectly flat granite.
clues: Its name translates as 'Pulpit Rock' — for its remarkably flat, square top that looks like a preacher's lectern.
It hangs 604 meters straight above a fjord, with no fence or barrier — visitors can stand right on the edge.
The cliff was formed about 10,000 years ago when glaciers cracked off massive blocks of rock during the last ice age.
It overlooks Lysefjord in southwestern Norway, near the city of Stavanger.
Preikestolen is in southwestern Norway.
puzzles.funFact: Despite its terrifying drop and total lack of guardrails, Preikestolen sees about 300,000 hikers a year — and remarkably few accidents. Local guides credit Norwegian culture's emphasis on personal responsibility (and good footwear).
puzzles.teaser: A flat slab of rock juts over a fjord. Nothing between you and the drop. Most people sit at the edge anyway.

puzzles.imageDescription: A jagged, pyramidal rocky island rises sharply from a stormy gray-blue Atlantic Ocean, its steep slopes covered in green moss and grass. Ancient stone beehive-shaped huts cluster near the rocky summit, accessible only by 600 steep stone steps cut into the cliff face. Thousands of seabirds wheel through the sky, and waves crash dramatically against the island's base. A second equally jagged peak rises nearby across rough waters.
clues: Tens of thousands of puffins nest on this island every summer, making it one of Europe's most important seabird breeding grounds.
Christian monks lived here in stone beehive huts from the 6th to the 13th century, surviving on fish, seabirds, and rainwater.
It featured prominently in 'Star Wars: The Force Awakens' as Luke Skywalker's hideout — a casting choice locals are still annoyed about.
It rises from the Atlantic about 12 km off Ireland's southwest Kerry coast.
Skellig Michael lies off Ireland's southwest coast.
puzzles.funFact: The 600 stone steps that climb Skellig Michael were cut by hand by 6th-century monks. They have no railings, are often slick with rain, and are still the only way up — a fact that makes them a controversial tourist destination today.
puzzles.teaser: Sixth-century monks climbed a sea-stack in the Atlantic and built beehive huts from stone. Luke Skywalker hid there too.

photo.description: a group of birds sitting on top of a rock

puzzles.imageDescription: A wide expanse of jet-black volcanic sand beach is bordered by towering basalt sea stacks rising from churning North Atlantic waves. Massive cliffs of geometric hexagonal basalt columns rise behind the beach, looking like petrified pipe organs. White surf crashes dramatically onto the dark sand, while puffins nest on the cliffs above. The whole scene has an otherworldly, almost monochromatic look.
clues: The black sand here was created by volcanic eruptions over millennia — and is so dark it absorbs heat aggressively in summer sun.
Its 'sneaker waves' are notoriously deadly — every few years a tourist is dragged out to sea by waves that arrive without warning.
Local Icelandic legend says its three offshore basalt sea stacks are trolls turned to stone by sunlight.
It lies on Iceland's south coast near the village of Vík.
Reynisfjara is on the south coast of Iceland.
puzzles.funFact: The basalt columns at Reynisfjara form because of how lava cools — slowly enough to crack into hexagons. The same physics created the Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland. They're visually identical, formed millions of years apart.
puzzles.teaser: The sand is black. The waves arrive without warning. The sea stacks are trolls who forgot to get home before sunrise.

puzzles.imageDescription: Endless rolling white sand dunes stretch to the horizon, dotted with thousands of crystal-clear blue, green, and turquoise rainwater lagoons that fill the valleys between the dunes. The pure white sand contrasts with the vivid pools of water under a brilliant blue sky. The lagoons appear and disappear seasonally with the rains. The surreal landscape looks like white sheets thrown across the ground — hence the name 'bedsheets'.
clues: Its name means 'bedsheets' in Portuguese — for the way the white dunes resemble linens spread across the land.
From May to September, rainwater fills 90,000 hectares of dunes with thousands of clear blue lagoons.
Despite resembling a desert, it isn't one — it gets up to 1,400 mm of rainfall per year.
It lies along the Atlantic coast in the northeastern Brazilian state of Maranhão.
Lençóis Maranhenses is a national park in northeastern Brazil.
puzzles.funFact: Some of the lagoons even contain fish — they survive the dry season buried in the mud. When the rains return and the lagoons reappear, they hatch back to life like a clockwork miracle.
puzzles.teaser: A desert that floods every year. White dunes fill with turquoise lagoons. Fish survive the dry season buried in the mud.

photo.description: body of water near snow covered land under calm blue sky

puzzles.imageDescription: A series of dazzling lakes in shades of blue, turquoise, emerald green, and aquamarine stretch through a forested alpine valley. Multi-tiered waterfalls cascade between the lakes, fed by glacial meltwater. Yellow autumn larch trees, evergreen pines, and snow-dusted peaks frame the otherworldly water colors. The lakes are so clear that submerged tree trunks are visible 20 meters down, and many appear to glow from within.
clues: Its lakes appear to glow from within — a result of crystal-clear glacial water and high mineral content reflecting light.
Local Tibetan and Qiang legend tells of a goddess who shattered her mirror — its 108 fragments became the valley's lakes.
It is home to giant pandas, golden snub-nosed monkeys, and Sichuan takin in the wild — though sightings are extremely rare.
It lies in the mountainous province of Sichuan in central China.
Jiuzhaigou Valley is in Sichuan, China.
puzzles.funFact: A 2017 earthquake severely damaged Jiuzhaigou's most famous waterfall. Surprisingly, scientists let nature take its course rather than rebuild — and four years later, new pools and cascades had formed in different shapes.
puzzles.teaser: The lakes glow from within — not from light, but from minerals. After an earthquake, nature rearranged itself and made new ones.

puzzles.imageDescription: A massive 200-meter tall rock monolith with vertical orange-tan cliff sides rises straight up from flat lush jungle, with ancient ruins visible on its summit. The rock features a steep, grand staircase ascending its face, including remnants of an enormous lion's paw structure marking what was once a fully sculpted lion's mouth entryway. Tropical greenery surrounds the dramatic outcrop on all sides.
clues: Built atop a 200-meter sheer rock pillar by a 5th-century king who feared his half-brother's revenge — and it didn't work; he was killed in a battle below.
Visitors enter the summit through what was once a giant lion's mouth carved from the rock — only its enormous paws survive today.
The rock walls partway up the cliff feature ancient frescoes of women — possibly the king's concubines, possibly celestial beings.
It rises from the dry zone of central Sri Lanka.
Sigiriya is in the dry zone of Sri Lanka.
puzzles.funFact: Sigiriya is sometimes called 'the eighth wonder of the world' — and the elaborate water gardens at its base are considered one of the oldest planned landscapes in the world, with hydraulics that still function 1,500 years later.
puzzles.teaser: A king who feared his brother built a palace on top of a two-hundred-metre rock. He was killed at the bottom of it.

photo.description: a large rock in the middle of a forest

puzzles.imageDescription: A vast otherworldly forest of jagged limestone pinnacles rises sharply from the ground, the razor-sharp gray rock formations standing 100 meters tall. Wooden walkways and rope bridges thread between the spiked stone columns, allowing visitors to traverse the labyrinthine landscape. Lush green vegetation grows in pockets between the stone teeth, and the unique habitat shelters lemurs and rare birds.
clues: Its name means 'where one cannot walk barefoot' — for limestone needles so sharp they can shred shoes.
Lemurs found nowhere else on Earth survive by leaping between razor-sharp limestone pinnacles 70+ meters high.
The formations are over 200 million years old — once an ancient seabed, gradually eroded into vertical cathedrals.
It lies on the western side of Madagascar, the world's fourth-largest island.
Tsingy de Bemaraha is in western Madagascar.
puzzles.funFact: The needles of Tsingy are so sharp that local guides require visitors to wear special harnesses and helmets. A fall onto the limestone has been compared to landing on a bed of meat-cleaver blades.
puzzles.teaser: A forest of razor-sharp limestone needles so dense that only flying lemurs can cross it. Every step draws blood.

photo.description: a group of people walking on a dirt road with tall trees with Avenue of the Baobabs in the background

puzzles.seed: famous mountain village inspired Spirited Away
puzzles.imageDescription: A historic mountainside village glowing in the dusk light, with red lanterns hanging in clusters along narrow steep stone-paved streets. Traditional teahouses with curved Asian eaves spill warm yellow light onto crowds. Stairways climb between cramped buildings on a steep mountain slope, with the dark shimmering ocean visible in the distance. Steam rises from food stalls.
clues: Hundreds of red lanterns illuminate its narrow stairway streets at night — a scene that reportedly inspired the bathhouse setting in Hayao Miyazaki's 'Spirited Away'.
It boomed during a late 19th-century gold rush, then nearly emptied — until 1989's film 'A City of Sadness' made it a tourist sensation.
Its terraced cliffside structure means walking is mostly up or down stone stairways — there are very few flat streets.
It overlooks the Pacific Ocean from the hills of northeastern Taiwan, an hour from Taipei.
Jiufen is in the hills of northeastern Taiwan.
puzzles.funFact: Jiufen's signature treat is taro balls — chewy starchy sweets sold by vendors who shape them by hand right before your eyes. Lines for the most famous shop wrap entirely around blocks on weekends.
puzzles.teaser: A gold rush built it. A film made it famous. A director from Tokyo saw it and made it into an animated dream.

photo.description: A bird's eye view of a small town in the mountains

puzzles.imageDescription: A horizontal slab of gray rock juts out 700 meters above a deep blue fjord, looking like a stone tongue protruding into thin air. Hikers stand at its very edge, dwarfed by the surrounding glacial valley with sheer mountain walls and patches of snow. The water far below appears bright turquoise from glacial sediment. The whole landscape feels primordial and immense.
clues: Its name means 'Troll's Tongue' — for the way a horizontal slab of cliff juts out 700 meters above the fjord like a giant stone tongue.
Reaching it requires a brutal 28 km round-trip hike — typically taking 10 to 12 hours, with thousands attempting it every summer.
The 'tongue' formed during the last ice age when the surrounding rock was eroded by glaciers, leaving the harder slab projecting outward.
It overlooks Lake Ringedalsvatnet in southwestern Norway.
Trolltunga is a cliff in southwestern Norway.
puzzles.funFact: The cliff was virtually unknown until around 2010, when Instagram made it a global icon. The trail wasn't even maintained — now thousands of hikers attempt it yearly, and rescue helicopters work overtime in summer.
puzzles.teaser: A slab of rock juts from a cliff face high above a fjord. For most of history, almost no one made the hike. Then social media arrived.

photo.description: a person standing on a rock in front of a lake with mountains in the background

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: White wings over a feudal hilltop — Japan's most intact samurai stronghold.
clues: Its walls are coated in white plaster, a deliberate choice that reflects heat, repels moisture, and gives it a nickname borrowed from a bird in flight.
This hilltop fortress survived every war, earthquake, and fire that swept through its city — partly through extraordinary engineering, partly through extraordinary luck.
Located in the Kansai region of Japan, it was never actually used in battle — its sheer presence was deterrent enough.
UNESCO designated it a World Heritage Site in 1993, calling it the finest surviving example of early 17th-century Japanese castle architecture.
Known as the White Heron Castle, it stands in Hyogo Prefecture and draws over a million visitors a year who climb its six-storey keep.
puzzles.funFact: During World War II, American firebombing destroyed much of the surrounding city, but Himeji Castle survived completely untouched — locals attributed it to a miracle, historians attribute it to the castle's isolated hilltop position.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: A dormant volcano encircled by a lagoon of impossible colour.
clues: The lagoon surrounding this island shifts from turquoise to deep emerald depending on depth — and the water is so clear that the coral formations below are visible from above.
A barrier reef encircles the island completely, creating a calm inner lagoon that has made it one of the most photographed places in the Pacific.
During World War II, American forces built an airstrip and supply base here, leaving behind artillery guns still visible on the hillsides today.
Its overwater bungalow concept — now copied across the world — was pioneered here in 1967 by hoteliers who received government permission to build directly above the lagoon.
Located in French Polynesia, this island is one of the world's most celebrated honeymoon destinations — its name in the local language may mean 'first-born.'
puzzles.funFact: Bora Bora's lagoon is technically a drowned volcanic caldera — the central mountain you see is just the rim of an ancient volcano, and the turquoise water fills what was once solid rock.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: Rome never left — a city of colonnaded streets and triumphal arches, still standing in the Middle East.
clues: This ancient city was buried under sand for centuries, which preserved it so completely that visitors today can walk on original paving stones worn smooth by chariot wheels.
It contains one of the most intact examples of Roman provincial city planning in the world — a colonnaded main street, two theatres, temples, and a hippodrome, all still standing.
The oval plaza at its entrance is unique in Roman architecture — no other city in the empire was built with an elliptical forum, and archaeologists still debate why it was designed this way.
Located in Jordan, it was part of the Decapolis — a league of ten Greco-Roman cities that served as cultural and commercial hubs on the eastern edge of the Roman Empire.

Every year it hosts a festival of Roman re-enactments in its hippodrome, where performers in period armour stage chariot races for modern audiences in one of the best-preserved Roman cities outside Italy.
puzzles.funFact: Jerash was so well preserved under sand that when excavated in the early 20th century, archaeologists found Roman-era inscriptions, mosaics, and graffiti scratched into walls by ancient visitors — including what appears to be a complaint about a bad meal.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: The world's largest tropical wetland — where jaguars hunt at the water's edge and the sky fills with macaws.
clues: This is the world's largest tropical wetland — an area larger than France that floods almost entirely each wet season, transforming from grassland to an inland sea.
It has the highest density of jaguars on Earth — because the open landscape allows researchers and tourists to actually see them, unlike dense jungle environments elsewhere.
Despite being one of the world's most biodiverse ecosystems, it receives a fraction of the conservation attention and tourism of better-known wilderness areas.
Located in central South America, primarily in Brazil with portions in Bolivia and Paraguay, it sits in a vast depression that collects water from the surrounding highlands each rainy season.
It is home to the giant anteater, giant river otter, hyacinth macaw, and capybara — the world's largest rodent — all found in densities that make wildlife sightings almost guaranteed.
puzzles.funFact: The Pantanal floods so dramatically that local ranchers have developed a unique cattle culture around it — their herds move seasonally to higher ground, following ancient routes used for centuries, making the Pantanal cowboy one of the last truly nomadic ranching traditions in the Americas.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: A path through green columns so tall they filter the light into something otherworldly.
clues: The Japanese government has formally listed the sound produced here as one of one hundred soundscapes worth preserving for future generations — a rustling, creaking chorus that no recording has ever captured faithfully.
The government of this country has listed the sound of wind through this grove as one of one hundred soundscapes worth preserving for future generations.
It sits on the western outskirts of a city that served as the imperial capital for over a thousand years.
Nearby are traditional rickshaw pullers, a monkey park, and one of the country's most famous Zen temples whose garden dates to the 14th century.
Located in the Arashiyama district of Kyoto, this bamboo path is one of the most photographed spots in Japan, best visited at dawn before the crowds arrive.
puzzles.funFact: The bamboo here grows so fast — up to 10cm per day — that workers must trim it constantly. Left unmanaged for even a season, it would swallow the paths entirely.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: A ceiling of living blue light — underground, in silence, drifting on black water.
clues: Visitors enter by boat and are instructed not to make a sound — any noise or vibration causes the light above them to go dark.
The light comes from living organisms — larvae of a species found almost nowhere else on Earth — that produce bioluminescence to attract prey into their silk threads.
From below, the cave ceiling looks like a night sky, with thousands of individual blue-white lights reflecting in still black water.
This cave system was first explored by a local Māori chief and a British surveyor in 1887, and the indigenous name for the area translates to 'hole in the rock.'
Located on New Zealand's North Island, these caves are one of the country's most visited natural attractions and the organisms that light them are found almost nowhere else on Earth.
puzzles.funFact: The glowworms are technically larvae of a fungus gnat species found almost exclusively here — they spend most of their lives in darkness glowing to hunt, then live only a few days as adults during which they do not eat at all.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: Twice as deep as the Grand Canyon — and condors ride its thermals at dawn.
clues: At over 3,270 metres deep, this is one of the deepest canyons on Earth — more than twice the depth of the Grand Canyon.
The Andean condor, with a wingspan of up to three metres, uses the canyon's thermal updrafts to soar without flapping — sometimes for hours at a time.
Pre-Inca terracing covers its walls, agricultural steps cut into near-vertical slopes that have been farmed continuously for over two thousand years.
It sits at an altitude that makes the air thin enough that visitors frequently need time to acclimatise before descending — and its walls are still farmed by descendants of the people who built them.

Located in southern Peru, this canyon is one of the best places on Earth to watch Andean condors soar at eye level at dawn — the world's largest flying birds rising on morning thermals just metres from the viewpoint edge.
puzzles.funFact: The terraces on Colca Canyon's walls were built by the Collagua and Cabana people before the Inca arrived — and the Inca, famous for their own terrace farming, were so impressed they incorporated the canyon into their empire without destroying what was already there.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: The world's oldest desert — its dunes are red, its coast is called the Skeleton Coast, and its fog is the only water some creatures ever drink.
clues: This desert is estimated to be between 55 and 80 million years old — making it the oldest desert on Earth, predating the dinosaurs' extinction.

Despite receiving almost no rainfall, it supports remarkable life because coastal fog rolls in from the cold ocean most mornings, providing moisture that beetles, lizards and plants have evolved to harvest.
Its sand dunes are among the tallest in the world — some exceeding 300 metres — and their colour ranges from pale yellow near the coast to deep brick-red further inland.
The wreck-strewn coastline on its western edge is called the Skeleton Coast, named for whale bones left by 19th-century whalers and the bleached remains of shipwrecked sailors.

Located in Namibia in southern Africa, its most famous landmark is a white clay pan surrounded by towering red dunes and dead trees that photographers travel from around the world to shoot at sunrise.
puzzles.funFact: The fog beetle of the Namib drinks by doing a headstand at dawn — its bumpy back collects fog droplets that roll down channels directly into its mouth. Engineers have studied it to design fog-harvesting water systems for dry regions.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: Pastel villages clinging to cliffs above a sea so blue it looks painted.
clues: The road running along this coastline is considered one of the most dangerous in Europe — narrow, cliffside, and shared between tour buses, scooters, and pedestrians.
Its towns were once maritime powers that rivalled Venice and Genoa — one of them had its own legal code that governed Mediterranean trade law for centuries.
Lemon groves cling to terraced hillsides above the sea, and the region produces a famous liqueur made from their zest that is exported worldwide.
Located in southern Italy, it was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997 and draws millions of visitors each summer to its clifftop villages.
The towns of Positano, Ravello, and Amalfi are its most famous stops — each stacked vertically up a cliff face with the sea visible from almost every window.
puzzles.funFact: The Amalfi Coast's famous limoncello liqueur was invented here in the early 20th century — though three different families claim credit for the original recipe, and the legal battle over the 'authentic' version has never been definitively resolved.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: Layered mountains that look spray-painted — red, orange, yellow, and purple banded like a geological cake.
clues: The colours here are entirely natural — the result of red sandstone and mineral deposits laid down over 24 million years, then folded and eroded into stripes.
The landscape is sometimes described as looking like an abstract painting — bands of crimson, gold, olive, and violet running horizontally across rounded hills.
It sits along the historic Silk Road, the ancient trade route connecting the Far East to Central Asia and beyond.
Located in northwestern China, it was largely unknown outside the country until a series of photographs went viral in the early 2000s and made it one of China's most surprising destinations.
This UNESCO World Heritage Geopark in Gansu Province is now one of China's most visually extraordinary natural attractions — and the colours intensify dramatically at sunrise and sunset.
puzzles.funFact: The intense red colour comes from iron oxide — essentially rust — in the sandstone. The same chemical that turns old nails red created one of the most vivid landscapes on Earth over tens of millions of years.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: Stone steps descending to a sacred river — where life, death, and ritual happen simultaneously at dawn.
clues: Every morning before sunrise, pilgrims descend stone steps to bathe in a river they consider the physical manifestation of a goddess.
The same riverbanks host cremation fires that burn continuously, day and night, year-round — families travel hundreds of kilometres to ensure their dead are cremated here.
This city is considered one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities on Earth, with some settlements dating back over 3,000 years.
Located on the banks of the Ganges in northern India, it is among the holiest cities in Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism simultaneously.
Its more than 80 ghats — stepped platforms leading to the river — each have different ritual functions, with one hosting a nightly fire ceremony that draws thousands of observers every evening.
puzzles.funFact: Mark Twain visited in 1896 and wrote: 'Benares is older than history, older than tradition, older even than legend, and looks twice as old as all of them put together.' The city's Sanskrit name means 'the city between two rivers.'

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: Vertical walls of rock dropping into black water — a fiord so dramatic it was used as Middle-earth.
clues: The sheer rock walls here rise more than a kilometre straight from the water — carved by glaciers over millions of years and flooded by the sea when the ice finally retreated.
A permanent layer of freshwater sits on top of the saltwater — from heavy rainfall — creating an eerie dark surface that tricks deep-sea creatures into living at snorkelling depth.
The rock faces are so steep and smooth that waterfalls appear from nowhere, plunging directly into the water below from sources invisible from the surface.
Peter Jackson filmed significant portions of the Lord of the Rings trilogy in the surrounding wilderness — the sheer scale of the landscape made it ideal for depicting a mythological world.
Located at the end of a single road in the southwest corner of New Zealand's South Island, this fiord was called the eighth wonder of the world by Rudyard Kipling.
puzzles.funFact: The freshwater layer floating on top of the saltwater blocks sunlight so effectively that black coral — normally a deep-sea species — grows at just 40 metres depth here, shallow enough for recreational divers to reach. It is one of the only places on Earth where this happens.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: A walled city of labyrinthine souks, where tanneries smell of saffron and pigeons scatter from minarets at dusk.
clues: The old city walls here are built from rammed earth mixed with lime — giving them a distinctive pink-red colour that has earned the city a famous nickname.
Inside, the souks are organized by trade: one street for spice merchants, another for leather workers, another for metalworkers — a system unchanged since medieval times.

The central square transforms completely between day and night: by afternoon it fills with snake charmers and storytellers; by evening it becomes one of the largest open-air food markets in the world.
Founded in 1070 by the Almoravid dynasty, it served as the capital of a Berber empire that stretched from Morocco to Spain.
Located at the foot of the Atlas Mountains in Morocco, its medina — the historic walled city — was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1985 and receives millions of visitors annually.
puzzles.funFact: Marrakech's famous central square — Jemaa el-Fnaa — has been continuously occupied by storytellers, musicians, and merchants for nearly a thousand years. UNESCO designated its oral traditions as an Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2001, the first public space ever to receive that distinction.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: The highest navigable lake in the world — and on it, islands built entirely from floating reeds.
clues: At 3,812 metres above sea level, this is the highest navigable lake in the world — large enough and deep enough that full-sized steamships have operated on it.
Some of its islands are entirely artificial — built and maintained by an indigenous people from totora reeds, which also serve as their primary building material, food source, and medicine.
In Inca cosmology, this lake was the birthplace of the sun and moon, and of the first Inca — making it one of the most sacred bodies of water in South America.
It straddles the border between Peru and Bolivia in the Andes, and both countries claim it as a national symbol.

The lake contains ancient ruins beneath its surface — submerged temples and roads discovered by archaeologists in the early 2000s suggesting civilizations far older than the Inca once lived on its shores.
puzzles.funFact: The Uros people have lived on their floating reed islands for centuries — and the islands themselves are alive. The reeds at the bottom rot continuously, so new layers must be added to the top regularly. An island is typically replaced entirely every 30 years.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: A city built downward — eight storeys below the earth, hidden beneath a Turkish village for centuries.
clues: This city descends eight storeys below the ground and could shelter up to 20,000 people — complete with ventilation shafts, wells, wine presses, stables, and churches.
Each level could be sealed from the inside by rolling enormous circular millstones across the doorways — designed so that invaders outside could not push them open.
It was carved into soft volcanic rock by early Christians hiding from persecution, and was used intermittently for over a thousand years whenever the surface became dangerous.
It was rediscovered entirely by accident in 1963 when a local man knocked down a wall in his basement and found a tunnel stretching further than he could see.
Located in central Turkey, it is the deepest of around 200 known underground settlements in the same region — the largest network of subterranean cities ever discovered.
puzzles.funFact: The ventilation shafts at Derinkuyu are so well designed that fresh air circulates to every level even 85 metres below the surface — the ancient engineers calculated airflow without any of the mathematics we would use today.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: A colonial city in a mountain valley — where mole sauce has seven versions and the dead are celebrated with marigolds.
clues: Seven distinct varieties of a single complex sauce were born in this city's kitchens — each a different colour, each made from over twenty ingredients, each recipe guarded by families as carefully as any legal document.

It is considered the culinary capital of its country — home to a complex dark sauce made from over 30 ingredients including chocolate and dried chillis, and a spirit distilled from agave that predates tequila by centuries.
Its Day of the Dead celebrations are considered among the most elaborate in the country — families camp overnight in cemeteries, building altars surrounded by marigolds to guide ancestors home.
An ancient hilltop city overlooks it from a flattened mountaintop — one of the earliest cities in Mesoamerica, occupied for over a thousand years before being abandoned.
Located in southern Mexico, its colonial centro histórico is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and its indigenous textiles and black clay pottery are recognized around the world.
puzzles.funFact: Oaxacan mole negro contains over 30 ingredients including chocolate, dried chillis, and charred tortilla — and takes up to three days to prepare properly. Each family guards its recipe as carefully as any legal document.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: Eighteen islands of green cliffs and no trees — where puffins outnumber people and the weather changes every hour.
clues: These islands have no native trees — the Norse settlers who arrived in the 9th century cleared the original birch forests, and the combination of wind and sheep has prevented their return ever since.
They are home to more puffins than people — the human population numbers around 55,000, while the seabird colonies number in the hundreds of thousands.
The grass on the rooftops here is not decoration — turf roofs provide insulation against the extreme Atlantic weather and have been used for centuries.
Located between Norway, Iceland, and Scotland in the North Atlantic, these islands are an autonomous territory of a Scandinavian country but have their own language, flag, and football team.

Located between Norway, Iceland, and Scotland, this autonomous North Atlantic territory is famous for its sheep-to-human ratio of nearly 2:1 — and for an underwater road roundabout, the only traffic circle in the world located beneath the sea.
puzzles.funFact: The Faroese word for the islands means 'sheep islands,' and there are more sheep than people: roughly 80,000 sheep to 55,000 humans. Sheep have the right of way on the roads.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: The hottest place on Earth — a landscape of acid pools, sulphur chimneys, and active lava lakes that looks like another planet.
clues: This place holds the record for the highest average annual temperature of any inhabited location on Earth — and it sits more than 100 metres below sea level.
The landscape includes pools of yellow and green acid, salt flats that shimmer like mirrors, and active hydrothermal vents that deposit chimneys of coloured minerals.
An active lava lake here — one of only a handful in the world — has been continuously erupting for over a century, filling the depression with an eerie red glow at night.
Located in the Afar region of Ethiopia near the borders of Eritrea and Djibouti, it is where three tectonic plates meet — and the continent of Africa is slowly pulling apart beneath it.

In 1974, just 200 kilometres from these acid pools, a scientist found the 3.2-million-year-old fossilised skeleton of 'Lucy' — one of our earliest known human ancestors — while a Beatles song played on a tape recorder in camp. The cradle of humanity sits in one of its most hostile places.
puzzles.funFact: The Danakil Depression is where Lucy — the famous 3.2-million-year-old Australopithecus skeleton that changed our understanding of human evolution — was discovered in 1974. The cradle of humanity sits in one of the most inhospitable places on Earth.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: A city built on water — where the market comes to you by boat before the sun is fully up.
clues: At dawn, vendors paddle wooden boats laden with fruit, vegetables, and steaming food through a floating market that has operated the same way for generations.
The city sits at the heart of a vast river delta where a great Asian river finally reaches the sea — its waterways are so dense that boats outnumber roads in some areas.
The surrounding delta produces enough rice to feed an entire nation and export tens of millions of tonnes annually — the fertile flatlands stretch to every horizon.
Located in southern Vietnam where river life and city life are inseparable, it is the largest city in the delta region and the gateway for most visitors exploring the waterways.
The floating markets here are considered among the most authentic in Southeast Asia — vendors hang samples of their produce from tall poles so buyers can identify what's on offer from a distance.
puzzles.funFact: The Mekong River carries so much sediment that the delta around Can Tho is actually growing — it extends further into the sea by about 30 metres every year. But rising sea levels and upstream dams are now reversing this, and parts of the delta are sinking for the first time in recorded history.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: A lakeside village so picturesque it inspired a replica in China — and has been inhabited for 7,000 years.
clues: This village clings to a narrow strip of land between a steep mountain and a deep lake — so constrained that for centuries, the only access was by boat.
Its salt mine, still operating today, is the oldest in the world — salt extracted here funded the Iron Age culture that archaeologists named after this very place.

In 2011, a Chinese company secretly photographed every corner of the village and built an exact replica in Guangdong Province — the villagers discovered this when tourists started arriving with printouts of the Chinese version.
Its church charnel house contains over 1,200 decorated skulls — when the graveyard ran out of space, bones were exhumed, bleached, painted with flowers and names, and displayed on shelves.
Located in Austria, this village of fewer than 800 permanent residents was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997 and now draws over a million visitors annually.
puzzles.funFact: The Hallstatt salt mine is so old that archaeologists have found perfectly preserved wooden tools, leather shoes, and even a Bronze Age backpack inside — kept intact for thousands of years by the antiseptic properties of the salt.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: The lowest point on Earth's surface — a lake so salty nothing can sink in it.
clues: This body of water is shrinking at a rate of more than one metre per year — sinkholes are appearing along its former shoreline as the water level drops.
Its salinity is nearly ten times that of the ocean — so high that fish cannot survive, and human swimmers cannot sink regardless of how they position their body.
The thick black mud from its shores has been used as a beauty treatment since the time of Cleopatra, who reportedly sourced it specifically for her skin care.
It sits at 430 metres below sea level — the lowest point on Earth's land surface — in a rift valley between two countries in the Middle East.
Ancient scrolls discovered in caves near its shores in 1947 — the oldest known manuscripts of the Hebrew Bible — transformed our understanding of ancient history and dated back over 2,000 years.
puzzles.funFact: The Dead Sea is getting saltier as it shrinks — evaporation removes water but leaves the salt behind. Scientists predict that at current rates, it could reach a concentration where salt crystals form on the surface, like what happened to parts of the Aral Sea.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: Karst peaks rising from a flat river valley — the landscape on the back of China's 20-yuan note.
clues: The landscape here formed over 300 million years as limestone dissolved and eroded into hundreds of sharp, forested peaks rising abruptly from flat farmland and river plains.
Cormorant fishermen still work this river using trained birds on leashes — a practice over a thousand years old, though today it is largely performed for tourists.
The scene is so iconic in its country that it was chosen to represent the nation on its 20-yuan banknote.
Located in the Guangxi region of southern China, the river cruise between its two main towns is considered one of the most scenic river journeys in Asia.
The town at the river's end has become a hub for rock climbing — the karst towers offer some of the most dramatic climbing terrain in the world above a village famous for its night market.
puzzles.funFact: The Li River's karst landscape inspired the floating mountains of Pandora in James Cameron's Avatar — Cameron's team visited the region specifically to photograph the peaks as reference material for the film's alien geology.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: A UNESCO town at the confluence of two rivers — where monks in saffron collect alms at dawn and French colonial buildings line the streets.
clues: Every morning before sunrise, hundreds of Buddhist monks walk silently through the streets collecting food offerings from local residents — a ceremony that has continued unbroken for centuries.

The streets here feel like two worlds collided and never separated — gilded temple rooftops rise above French colonial shophouses, and saffron-robed monks pass whitewashed facades with shuttered windows.
Temple compounds outnumber city blocks here — this town has more than thirty active wats within walking distance of each other, each with resident monks who maintain them daily.

Located in a landlocked country in Southeast Asia, it was designated a UNESCO World Heritage City in 1995 — one of the first in the region — in recognition of its remarkably intact traditional architecture.

A short drive away, the Kuang Si waterfall cascades through turquoise travertine pools bright enough to look artificial — and at the forest above it, a sanctuary rescues sun bears confiscated from the illegal wildlife trade.
puzzles.funFact: The tak bat alms ceremony has become so popular with tourists that UNESCO has issued warnings about its commercialization — some monks have stopped participating because tourists photograph them with flash cameras at close range during the silent predawn ritual.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: The end of the world — an archipelago of glaciers, peat bogs, and penguin colonies where the wind never stops.
clues: This place sits at the southern tip of the Americas — so remote that the city here bills itself as the southernmost in the world, and ships heading to Antarctica pass through its waters.
It was named by Ferdinand Magellan in 1520 when he saw fires lit by the indigenous people along the shoreline as his fleet passed through the strait that now bears his name.
Darwin visited during his voyage on the Beagle and was so struck by the indigenous people here that his observations shaped his thinking about human adaptation to extreme environments.
It is split between two countries — Argentina to the east and Chile to the west — divided by a straight line that makes it one of the most unusual borders on Earth.

Located at the southern tip of South America, its main Argentine city — Ushuaia, which bills itself as the southernmost city in the world — sits on the shores of a wide bay surrounded by mountains and is the gateway for most Antarctic expedition cruises.
puzzles.funFact: The Yaghan people who lived here for thousands of years wore almost no clothing despite temperatures near freezing — they coated themselves in animal fat and kept fires burning constantly, including in their canoes. Darwin was astonished; the Yaghan found his clothing absurd.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: Pale limestone towers turning pink at sunset — the Alps' most dramatic skyline.
clues: These mountains glow pink and orange at sunset and sunrise — a phenomenon caused by the pale rock catching low-angle light, and it has a name in the local dialect that translates roughly as 'turning rosy.'
They formed from ancient coral reefs — what are now peaks over 3,000 metres high were once flat seabed, and fossil seashells are still found near the summits.

During World War I, the front line ran through these mountains — soldiers on both sides tunnelled into the glaciers and detonated explosives inside the rock, and bodies are still being recovered from melting ice today.
Located in northeastern Italy near the Austrian border, they are a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of Europe's premier ski destinations in winter.
The Three Peaks — three vertical towers of pale rock rising from a high plateau — are their most iconic formation, appearing on postcards and climbing magazines worldwide.
puzzles.funFact: The mineral dolomite — which gives these mountains their name and colour — was identified here by French geologist Déodat Gratet de Dolomieu in 1788. He noticed the rock didn't fizz when acid was applied, unlike normal limestone, and realized it was a previously unknown mineral.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: A nation of coral rings in the Indian Ocean — the lowest country on Earth, threatened by the sea that surrounds it.
clues: This nation consists of 26 atolls and over 1,000 coral islands — but its average elevation above sea level is less than one metre, making it the lowest-lying country on Earth.
Scientists predict that without intervention, most of its islands could be uninhabitable by 2100 due to rising sea levels — making it the most climate-vulnerable nation on the planet.
It was the first country in the world to hold a cabinet meeting underwater — in 2009, the president and ministers donned scuba gear to sign a document calling for global carbon emission reductions.
Located in the Indian Ocean southwest of Sri Lanka, it is the smallest country in Asia by land area but one of the most spread-out — its islands stretch across 900 kilometres of ocean.

Its luxury overwater resorts have made it synonymous with honeymoon travel — though the government is quietly purchasing land in neighbouring countries as a potential relocation site for its entire population.
puzzles.funFact: The Maldives has a contingency plan: the government has been purchasing land in Australia, India, and Sri Lanka as a potential relocation site for its entire population if the islands become uninhabitable. The country is preparing for its own disappearance.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: A city of vintage cars, crumbling baroque facades, and music spilling from every doorway.
clues: The streets here are filled with American cars from the 1950s — kept running through improvisation and ingenuity for decades after a trade embargo made new parts impossible to obtain.
Its old city centre is one of the best-preserved colonial urban areas in the Americas, with Spanish baroque buildings dating to the 16th century.
The city was founded by the Spanish in 1519 and grew wealthy as the staging point for treasure fleets carrying gold and silver from the Americas back to Europe.
Its seafront promenade is famous as a gathering place where locals sit at dusk watching the sun drop into the water — and the sea spray regularly soaks anyone sitting too close to the wall.
A famous American author lived here for nearly 20 years and his favourite bar still serves the drink he reportedly consumed daily — a bronze statue of him stands at the spot where he always stood.
puzzles.funFact: Cuba has more classic American cars per capita than any country in the world — including the United States. When the embargo began in 1962, there were about 150,000 American cars in Cuba. There are still roughly 60,000 operating today, maintained entirely without American spare parts.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: The world's largest intact volcanic caldera — a self-contained ecosystem where predator and prey live on the same stage.
clues: This is the largest intact volcanic caldera on Earth — a collapsed volcano whose walls form a natural enclosure about 20 kilometres across and 600 metres deep.
The crater walls are steep enough that most large animals do not leave — creating a self-sustaining ecosystem with one of the highest predator densities anywhere in Africa.
It contains one of the densest concentrations of wildlife on the continent: lions, elephants, rhinos, hippos, flamingos, and wildebeest all share a space smaller than some cities.
Located in northern Tanzania, it was formed by a massive volcanic collapse roughly 2 to 3 million years ago and is part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
It is one of the few places on Earth where you can see lion, elephant, buffalo, black rhinoceros, and hippopotamus — five of Africa's most iconic species — in a single day.
puzzles.funFact: The lions of Ngorongoro are genetically distinct from lions elsewhere in Africa — centuries of living within the crater walls has made them more inbred than any other lion population on Earth. Scientists monitor them closely because their limited gene pool makes them vulnerable to disease.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: Emerald steps carved into a hillside — an ancient irrigation system so sophisticated it shapes an entire culture.
clues: Curved terraces of vivid green descend a hillside in concentric rings, each level flooded so it mirrors the sky — and the entire system has been governed not by engineers or governments but by a hierarchy of water temples for over a thousand years.

This system is not just agricultural — it is governed by spiritual principles that coordinate sharing between farmers across an entire landscape, and has operated continuously for over a thousand years.
UNESCO inscribed this landscape as a World Heritage Site in 2012, recognising it as a living cultural tradition that has shaped both the land and the society simultaneously.
Located in the cultural heartland of an Indonesian island where traditional dance, painting, and temple ceremony have been practiced without interruption for centuries.

The deep green of the terraces against red earth and palm trees has made this one of the most photographed landscapes in Southeast Asia — and the irrigation system behind it is as ingenious as the view.
puzzles.funFact: The subak irrigation system is so effective at pest control that when the World Bank convinced Balinese farmers to abandon it in the 1970s in favour of modern farming methods, pest populations exploded. Within a decade, the traditional system was restored — and pest outbreaks stopped.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: A walled city on the Caribbean — where Spanish gold once left for Europe and bougainvillea spills over every colonial balcony.
clues: This city is enclosed by a massive colonial wall — built over decades by the Spanish to protect the most important port in the Americas, through which nearly all the gold and silver looted from the continent passed.
Its historic centre is a maze of narrow cobblestone streets where brightly coloured buildings with flower-draped balconies have remained largely unchanged since the 16th century.
It was attacked repeatedly by pirates and privateers — Francis Drake sacked it in 1586, and the Spanish responded by building fortifications that took over 200 years to complete.
Located on the Caribbean coast of Colombia, its old city and fortifications were designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1984 and are considered the best-preserved colonial port in the Americas.
Gabriel García Márquez set several of his novels here and lived in the city until his death, calling it the most beautiful city in the world.
puzzles.funFact: The walls of Cartagena took so long to build — over 200 years — that by the time they were finished, the era of pirate attacks was essentially over. Spain spent enormous treasure protecting treasure that had largely already been spent.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a city split by a gorge and bridged by centuries of ambition
clues: A city perched on the edge of a sheer cliff, cleaved in two by a dramatic gorge dropping nearly 100 metres to the river far below.
Its whitewashed buildings and iron balconies overlook rugged inland mountains shaped by centuries of Moorish and Christian contest.
During the Spanish Civil War, captured prisoners were thrown from the cliff into the gorge below — a scene Ernest Hemingway witnessed and documented in his writing.
Located in Andalusia, southern Spain, it gave birth to the modern tradition of bullfighting on foot, and its most iconic sight is the 300-year-old Puente Nuevo bridge.
Orson Welles was so enchanted by this cliffside Andalusian city that he requested his ashes be buried here — on a local bullfighter's estate, where they remain.
puzzles.funFact: Orson Welles visited Ronda obsessively throughout his life and asked to be buried there. His ashes now rest on a bullfighter's estate in the Andalusian hills — a man who made his name in Hollywood, permanently interred in a Spanish cliff-city.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a river that loses itself in the sands — and becomes something extraordinary
clues: A vast inland labyrinth of papyrus channels, lily-covered lagoons, and flooded islands that appears from above like a mosaic of blue and green.
The river feeding it flows not to the ocean but disappears into desert sand, creating a delta that blooms inland every year — a flood arriving paradoxically in the dry season.
Elephants, hippos, wild dogs, and lions all converge on this maze of waterways — one of the last places on Earth where the full suite of African megafauna gathers in one landscape.
A UNESCO World Heritage Site in southern Africa, it sits in a landlocked country home to over a third of the world's elephants.
The Okavango River floods this Botswanan delta each year after rains fall in faraway Angola — the water takes four months to travel here, blooming the Kalahari just when it needs it most.
puzzles.funFact: The Okavango Delta is the only major river system on Earth that flows away from the ocean — it starts in Angola, travels over 1,000 km, and then simply disappears into the Kalahari sand without ever reaching the sea.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to the oldest and deepest lake on Earth
clues: A vast crescent carved by ancient tectonic forces holds within its depths more liquid freshwater than any lake on Earth — its floor plunging so far down it sits below sea level.
In winter, its surface freezes into transparent blue ice metres thick — local tribes once drove across it by horse-drawn sled for months at a time.
It holds about 20% of the world's unfrozen surface freshwater and is home to a freshwater seal found nowhere else on Earth.
Situated in Siberia, Russia, this rift lake is geologically ancient — over 25 million years old — and surrounded by mountains and taiga forest.
Lake Baikal is the world's deepest lake at 1,642 metres, containing more freshwater than all of North America's Great Lakes combined.
puzzles.funFact: Lake Baikal's nerpa seal evolved there independently from any ocean species — it is the only exclusively freshwater seal on Earth, and scientists still debate how its ancestors reached this landlocked Siberian lake millions of years ago.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to an ancient Nabataean city carved into rose-red cliffs — Saudi Arabia's first UNESCO World Heritage Site
clues: More than 100 monumental tombs are carved directly into sandstone outcrops rising from a flat desert plain — their facades elaborately decorated despite the emptiness surrounding them.
The civilisation that built this place also built a more famous city to the north, connected by ancient trade routes carrying incense, spices, and silk across the Arabian peninsula.
