For centuries it was sealed from the outside world — foreigners were forbidden entry, and the site sat largely unknown to travellers until it opened to tourism for the first time in 2020.
Located in the Al-Ula region of northwestern Saudi Arabia, it was the southern capital of the Nabataean kingdom, the same civilisation that built Petra in present-day Jordan.

Hegra — also known as Madain Saleh — became Saudi Arabia's first UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008, and its 111 carved tombs are better preserved than those at Petra because the site remained sealed for so long.
puzzles.funFact: Hegra's tombs are more intact than Petra's because Saudi Arabia kept the site completely closed to outsiders for centuries — the isolation that made it unknown is precisely what preserved it so perfectly.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a fortress-palace that rises from its mountain like a continuation of the rock itself
clues: A thirteen-storey structure of whitewashed stone and red chapels climbs a rocky hill with a gravity that suggests it grew there rather than was built.
Its walls contain thousands of gilded statues, jewel-encrusted shrines, and sacred objects accumulated across centuries of continuous religious devotion.
Construction began in the 7th century and continued for decades — later rulers expanded it room by room, corridor by corridor, until it contained over 1,000 chambers.
For centuries the winter residence of the Dalai Lamas, it sits in Lhasa in the Tibet Autonomous Region of China.
The Potala Palace in Lhasa was the political and spiritual heart of Tibet, housing 13 Dalai Lamas and containing the gilded tombs of 8 of them.
puzzles.funFact: No complete inventory of the Potala Palace has ever been made — it contains over 1,000 rooms, and curators believe there are chambers that have not been entered in living memory.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a monastery that clings to a cliff face like a dream refusing to fall
clues: A cluster of white and golden buildings clings impossibly to a vertical granite cliff, connected by a steep forested path winding through mountain mist.
The buildings are anchored directly into the rock face with no flat foundation — monks have lived and prayed here at altitude for over three centuries, sustained by supplies carried up by mule.
No one fully understands how it was built — the cliff face it occupies has no natural ledge, and the construction methods used in the 17th century remain a subject of scholarly debate.
It sits in the Paro Valley of Bhutan, a tiny Himalayan kingdom that measures its success in Gross National Happiness rather than GDP.
Paro Taktsang — the Tiger's Nest Monastery — perches 900 metres above the Paro Valley floor; legend says a guru flew here on a tigress to meditate in the cave it was built to honour.
puzzles.funFact: The Tiger's Nest was largely destroyed by fire in 1998 and rebuilt so faithfully that most visitors cannot tell — the reconstruction used the same materials and traditional techniques as the 17th-century original, completed in just four years.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to an Arctic archipelago where polar bears outnumber people
clues: A jagged archipelago of glaciers, tundra, and coal-black mountains sits at the edge of the navigable world, where the sky burns green or glows amber for months at a time.
Polar bears roam freely here — so freely that residents are required to carry rifles when venturing beyond the settlement limits.
Despite sitting at 78° north latitude, a warm ocean current keeps it navigable for much of the year, making it a base for polar expeditions since the 17th century.
An autonomous Norwegian territory, its main settlement Longyearbyen is one of the northernmost permanent communities on Earth.
Svalbard is home to the Global Seed Vault — a doomsday backup of over 1.3 million seed samples buried deep in permafrost to protect humanity's food supply.
puzzles.funFact: It is technically illegal to die in Longyearbyen, Svalbard — because bodies do not decompose in the permafrost, residents who are gravely ill are flown to the mainland to die there instead.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to an ancient city whose marble streets once echoed with a million footsteps
clues: Colonnaded marble streets stretch toward a hillside, lined with the eroded facades of libraries, bathhouses, and temples built for gods long since forgotten.
The city once had a sophisticated sewer system, heated floors, and a library holding 12,000 scrolls — feats of engineering that vanished with the empire that built them.
Its Great Theatre, carved into the hillside, held 25,000 spectators and was where the Apostle Paul reportedly caused a riot preaching against idol worship.
Located on the Aegean coast of modern-day Turkey, it was once the second-largest city in the Roman Empire after Rome itself.
Ephesus was home to the Temple of Artemis — one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, now reduced to a single reconstructed column in a muddy field.
puzzles.funFact: Ephesus had ancient 'advertisements' carved into the pavement — a footprint, a woman's face, and a heart pointing toward the city's brothel, so visiting sailors who didn't speak the language could still find their way.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a misty highland park where the rarest great apes on Earth look you in the eye
clues: Dense bamboo gives way to ancient hagenia forest on a series of volcanic slopes, where mist clings to the canopy and the silence is broken only by cracking branches.

Trekkers here spend hours hiking to reach a gorilla family, then sit within metres of them for a full hour — one of the only places on Earth where sustained contact with wild great apes is a regular experience.
Dian Fossey lived and worked on these slopes for 18 years, was murdered here in 1985, and chose to be buried in the gorilla graveyard she created — among the animals she gave her life to protect.
Located in northwestern Rwanda on the slopes of the Virunga volcano chain, a single trekking permit costs $1,500 — revenue that has directly funded a rare conservation success story.
Volcanoes National Park holds roughly half the world's remaining mountain gorillas — fewer than 1,100 survive in the wild, making them one of the most endangered great apes on Earth.
puzzles.funFact: Mountain gorilla numbers have actually increased in recent decades — the only great ape population currently growing — because trekking permit revenue of $1,500 per person funds anti-poaching patrols so effectively that the gorillas are safer now than at any point in the past century.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a medieval walled city cradled between dark mountains and a glassy Adriatic bay
clues: Stone walls climb the steep mountain directly behind a perfectly preserved old town, their switchbacks visible for kilometres as they ascend toward a ruined fortress.
The bay enclosing the city is so deep and sheltered it was long mistaken for a fjord — its calm water mirrors the grey limestone cliffs above.
Venetian-era palaces, Romanesque churches, and cats — hundreds of them — define the labyrinthine streets inside these ancient fortifications.
Situated on the Bay of Kotor in Montenegro, it is one of the best-preserved medieval cities on the Adriatic and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Kotor's famous city walls stretch for 4.5 kilometres and climb 260 metres up the mountainside — hiking the full circuit takes about an hour.
puzzles.funFact: Kotor is so famous for its cats that the city has a dedicated Cat Museum and sells cat-themed souvenirs at nearly every stall — the animals have been considered sacred protectors of the old town since Venetian sailors brought them on ships centuries ago.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to an Inca citadel so remote that fewer people visit it in a year than Machu Picchu sees in an hour
clues: Stone terraces cascade down a mountain ridge above a roaring river canyon, the stonework precise and proud despite centuries of encroaching jungle.
The approach requires a two-day trek through dramatic mountain scenery — there is no road, no cable car, and no shortcut to this citadel.
Archaeologists estimate only 30 to 40 percent of this site has been excavated — more ruins lie under the jungle than have ever been seen by modern eyes.
Located in southern Peru near Cusco, it shares its architectural DNA with Machu Picchu — the same precision stonework and sacred alignment with the peaks above.
Choquequirao receives fewer than 30,000 visitors per year — compared to over a million at Machu Picchu — because reaching it requires a gruelling multi-day trek with no road access.
puzzles.funFact: During the Spanish conquest, the last Inca rulers used Choquequirao as a refuge and are believed to have brought enormous quantities of gold there — which was never surrendered to the Spanish and has never been found. It may still be somewhere beneath the jungle.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to the highest peak in a land of glaciers, lakes, and sky
clues: A pyramid of ice-raked rock rises above a valley of turquoise glacial rivers, its summit so frequently shrouded in cloud that local people believed it touched the sky.
On its flanks lies the Tasman Glacier — the longest glacier in the Southern Hemisphere outside Antarctica, calving icebergs into a milky blue lake at its terminal face.
Edmund Hillary trained on these glaciers and slopes before becoming the first person to summit Everest — the mountain prepared him for everything that followed.
Located in the Southern Alps on New Zealand's South Island, it is the country's highest peak and sacred to the Māori who call it 'Cloud Piercer'.
Aoraki Mount Cook lost about ten metres from its summit in a 1991 rockfall that dumped 14 million cubic metres of debris onto the Tasman Glacier below.
puzzles.funFact: Aoraki Mount Cook is one of the only mountains in the world with two official names of fully equal legal standing — 'Aoraki' in Māori and 'Mount Cook' in English — after a 1998 treaty between the New Zealand government and the local iwi.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to the world's largest car-free urban area — an ancient city that has barely changed in a thousand years
clues: Nine thousand narrow alleyways thread between tanneries, madrasas, and souks in a labyrinth so dense that sunlight barely reaches the cobblestones below.
The smell hits before the sight — the pungent, medieval aroma of dye, leather, and spice rising from a city that has worked the same trades for centuries.
The medina is so labyrinthine that even locals use the overlapping calls to prayer from dozens of mosques to orient themselves — sound is the city's navigation system.
Located in northern Morocco, this medina is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and home to the world's oldest continuously operating university, founded in 859 AD.
Fes el-Bali's famous leather tanneries — where hides are soaked in pigeon dung and dyed in honeycomb pots of colour — have operated continuously since the 11th century.
puzzles.funFact: The University of al-Qarawiyyin in Fes was founded in 859 AD by a woman named Fatima al-Fihri — recognised by UNESCO as the world's oldest continuously operating university, predating Oxford by over 200 years.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a landscape powered from below — where the Earth itself breathes
clues: The ground here is warm underfoot; rainbow-ringed pools of boiling water punctuate a landscape that hisses, steams, and erupts on a schedule of its own.
Bison graze at the edge of geothermal vents, seemingly indifferent to the fact that they stand above one of the largest supervolcanoes on the planet.
It is home to the largest free-roaming bison herd in North America — descendants of the last wild herd to survive the 19th-century mass slaughter that killed 60 million of them.
The world's first national park, established in 1872 in the western United States, it protects more than half of the world's geysers within its borders.
Its most famous geyser erupts every 90 minutes to a height of 50 metres — so reliably that the National Park Service posts predicted eruption times, accurate to within 10 minutes.
puzzles.funFact: Old Faithful has been erupting for centuries and has never once missed its schedule by more than 20 minutes — the National Park Service posts predicted eruption times based on the duration of the previous eruption, a geological clock accurate enough to set your watch by.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a golden temple that feeds 100,000 people every single day — for free
clues: A gleaming golden structure rises from the centre of a sacred pool of still water, reached by a marble causeway where pilgrims walk barefoot through the early morning silence.
The complex runs one of the largest free kitchens on Earth — every visitor regardless of faith or status is fed without charge, day and night.
Its four doors, one facing each direction, symbolise the acceptance of all people from all corners of the world — no religion, caste, or class is turned away.
Located in Amritsar in the Punjab region of India, it is the holiest shrine of the Sikh faith and a symbol of radical equality and service.
The Golden Temple — Sri Harmandir Sahib — is plated with 750 kilograms of pure gold, donated by Maharaja Ranjit Singh in the early 19th century.
puzzles.funFact: The Golden Temple's langar — community kitchen — serves free meals to between 50,000 and 100,000 people every single day, run entirely by volunteers and donations. It has never once closed in its history, including during wars and pandemics.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a city that produces more hot spring water than anywhere else on Earth — a place where the ground itself is alive
clues: Steam rises from drains, pavements, and roadside vents throughout this city — an almost permanent mist that gives even ordinary streets an otherworldly quality.
Its eight geothermal pools — known locally as the 'Hells' — range from blood-red to brilliant cobalt blue, each a different mineral composition, each at near-boiling point.
The city produces over 130,000 tonnes of hot spring water every day — more than any other city on Earth — used for cooking, bathing, heating homes, and even cooking eggs in the steam.
Located on the island of Kyushu in Japan, it has been a pilgrimage destination for hot spring bathers for over a thousand years.
Beppu's most famous pool — Chinoike Jigoku, or 'Blood Pond Hell' — gets its vivid red colour from iron in the water and has been boiling continuously at 78°C for over six centuries.
puzzles.funFact: Beppu residents cook food using nothing but geothermal steam — a local tradition called 'jigoku mushi' (hell steaming) that uses the city's natural heat to prepare vegetables, eggs, and even puddings in wooden steamers placed directly over ground vents.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a plateau scattered with thousands of ancient stone vessels whose purpose remains a mystery
clues: Thousands of enormous stone cylinders — some taller than a person and weighing several tonnes — are scattered across a highland plateau like discarded cups of giants.
They were carved over 2,000 years ago by a civilisation that left no written records — their purpose is still debated: funeral urns, rice wine vats, or rainwater collectors.
The plateau around them is pocked with bomb craters — this landscape was one of the most heavily bombed places on Earth during the 1960s, and unexploded ordnance still makes some sites off-limits.
Located in Xieng Khouang province in northern Laos, the site was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2019.
The Plain of Jars in Laos contains over 2,000 stone jars across 90 sites — and no one knows for certain who made them, when exactly, or why.
puzzles.funFact: Laos is the most heavily bombed country per capita in history — the US dropped more bombs on it during the Vietnam War era than on all of Europe in World War II combined, and an estimated 30% of them never exploded and still kill people today.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a volcanic lake so beautiful that Aldous Huxley called it 'the most beautiful lake in the world'
clues: Three towering volcanoes preside over a deep caldera lake, their reflections trembling in water that shifts from brilliant blue to silver depending on the hour.
A dozen indigenous Maya villages cling to its shores, each with its own distinct textile traditions and Mayan dialect, reachable only by motorboat across the shimmering water.
The lake has no natural outlet — it drains entirely through porous volcanic rock — and its depth has never been reliably measured, with estimates ranging from 200 to over 340 metres.
Located in the Guatemalan Highlands of Central America at 1,562 metres elevation, it is considered sacred by the surrounding Maya communities and formed by a supervolcanic eruption 84,000 years ago.
Aldous Huxley visited and declared it the most beautiful lake in the world — a quote in every guidebook ever written — and divers have since found submerged ancient Maya temples on its floor.
puzzles.funFact: Divers exploring Lake Atitlán's floor have found submerged ancient Maya ruins — temples and ceremonial structures flooded when the lake level rose, now visible only to those who descend into the blue-green depths.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a Silk Road city so intact it feels like time stopped five centuries ago
clues: Terracotta walls encircle a compact maze of mosques, minarets, and madrasas, all in the same sandy palette as the desert surrounding them on every side.
The main minaret here was never completed — it was intended to be the tallest in the region, but the emir died before it reached its planned height and no one dared finish it.
Families inside the inner walled city trace their ancestry directly to the Silk Road merchants and craftsmen who lived here centuries ago — the same trades, the same streets, the same families.
Located in the Khorezm region of Uzbekistan, near the Amu Darya River that once fed the now-vanishing Aral Sea, it was a key trading post on the ancient Silk Road.
Khiva's Itchan Kala — the inner walled city — was the first Uzbek site added to the UNESCO World Heritage list, recognised in 1990 as one of the finest surviving examples of Islamic urban planning.
puzzles.funFact: Khiva's Kalta Minor minaret was supposed to be visible from Bukhara, 500 km away — an architectural ego trip cut short when the commissioning emir died, and the project stopped forever, leaving a wide, squat stump that is now the city's most recognisable structure.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to the city where Africa and Brazil fused to create a culture unlike anywhere else on Earth
clues: Brightly coloured colonial buildings line the cobblestones of a hilltop old town overlooking a vast bay — the largest in the Americas — where the Atlantic light is extraordinary at every hour.
The music here is inescapable — percussion-heavy, syncopated rhythms born from three centuries of African influence that permeate the streets, bars, and churches in equal measure.
It was the first capital of a great colonial empire and the port through which more enslaved Africans arrived than any other city in the Americas — a history that shaped every aspect of its culture.
Located on a peninsula in the state of Bahia in northeastern Brazil, its historic centre Pelourinho is a UNESCO World Heritage Site of vivid Portuguese colonial and Afro-Brazilian architecture.
Salvador's Carnival is the largest street party on Earth — bigger than Rio's by attendance — drawing over two million people to the streets for a week of Afro-Brazilian music and celebration.
puzzles.funFact: More enslaved Africans arrived in Salvador than in any other city in the Americas — over 1.5 million people — which is why Salvador today has the largest African-descended population outside Africa, and why its food, music, religion, and dance are more African than Portuguese.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a medieval Flemish city so preserved that film directors use it as a real-life movie set
clues: Stepped gable houses in ochre, brick red, and pale gold line a network of calm canals, their reflections shimmering below carved stone bridges.
Swans drift past chocolate shops and breweries in a city whose entire medieval centre has barely changed in 600 years.
It was once the trading capital of northern Europe — ships from Venice, Genoa, and England docked here before the harbour silted up and commerce moved elsewhere.
Located in the Flanders region of Belgium, its historic centre is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the finest examples of Flemish Gothic architecture anywhere.

Bruges became accidentally preserved — its harbour river silted up in the 15th century, cutting off trade, freezing the city in time, and inadvertently creating one of Europe's most perfectly intact medieval centres.
puzzles.funFact: For four centuries after trade collapsed, Bruges was too economically depressed to afford renovation — no developer wanted to invest, no city council had funds to modernise. Poverty turned out to be the most effective preservation policy in history.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a smouldering crater rising from a sea of sand in the middle of a vast volcanic caldera
clues: A perfectly conical volcano, its crater rim wreathed in sulphurous smoke, rises from a pale grey 'sea of sand' — a flat ash plain stretching to the encircling caldera walls.
The ash plain surrounding it is so otherworldly that horses are hired to carry visitors across it — a surreal procession of riders dwarfed by the smoking mountain ahead.
The Tenggerese people have lived on the slopes of this active volcano for centuries and have never left — they believe the mountain is their ancestor and that it will never harm them.
Located in East Java, Indonesia, it sits within the Tengger Caldera — a collapsed ancient supervolcano — and remains one of the country's most visited and most active volcanoes.
Mount Bromo's annual Yadnya Kasada festival sees the Tenggerese climb to the crater rim and throw offerings — livestock, vegetables, money — directly into the smouldering volcanic mouth.
puzzles.funFact: During the Yadnya Kasada festival, the Tenggerese throw live chickens, vegetables, and money into the active volcanic crater as offerings — and locals scramble down the inner slopes trying to catch the offerings before they fall in, believing anything caught carries the mountain's blessing.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a Baltic walled city so perfectly preserved it looks like a film set for the Middle Ages
clues: Conical towers and stepped gable rooftops rise behind a ring of medieval walls, the old city perched on a limestone plateau above a deep natural harbour.
Cobbled alleyways between sandstone and limestone buildings lead to a hilltop cathedral and the ramparts of a 13th-century fortress — all in continuous use today.
The old town survived Soviet occupation completely intact — modernisation programmes that transformed every other major Baltic city somehow left this one untouched.
The capital of Estonia, on the Baltic Sea, it was a Hanseatic League city — one of a network of prosperous medieval trading ports stretching from London to Novgorod.
Tallinn Old Town is so intact that its medieval pharmacy — opened in 1422 — is still operating today, making it one of the oldest continuously running pharmacies in the world.
puzzles.funFact: Tallinn's Town Hall Pharmacy has been operating continuously since 1422 — over 600 years — making it one of the oldest pharmacies in the world still serving customers from the same address.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to the largest ancient religious complex ever built — added to by 30 consecutive pharaohs over 2,000 years
clues: A forest of columns nearly 20 metres tall fills a hall so vast that Notre-Dame Cathedral could fit inside it with room to spare — and this is just one room in a complex of dozens.
It took over 2,000 years and 30 consecutive rulers to build — each adding their own hall, obelisk, or statue, each competing to outdo the previous dynasty in scale and grandeur.
Every pharaoh who built here also chiselled out their predecessor's name and replaced it with their own — the entire complex is a monument to three millennia of competitive royal ego.
Located near Luxor on the east bank of the Nile in Egypt, it was the most important place of worship in the ancient Egyptian world for over two thousand years.
Karnak is the world's second-largest ancient religious site after Angkor Wat — and its sacred lake, used by priests for purification rituals, is still filled with water today.
puzzles.funFact: Karnak's sacred lake has been continuously full of water for over 3,000 years — fed by groundwater seeping from the Nile — a feat of ancient hydraulic engineering that still works perfectly today without any modern maintenance.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to the world's most accessible active volcano — where you can stand at the rim and watch the Earth roar
clues: The glow is visible from the ocean at night — a smouldering summit that hurls incandescent rocks into the air dozens of times a day, reliably, like clockwork.
Unlike most active volcanoes, a dirt track leads almost to the summit — visitors walk the final slope on foot and reach the crater edge where the lava lake erupts every few minutes.
It has been erupting continuously for at least 800 years — one of the longest documented continuous eruptions on Earth — and the local indigenous people consider it their ancestral god.
Located on the island of Tanna in the Pacific archipelago nation of Vanuatu, it is one of the most visited attractions in Melanesia.
Mount Yasur is nicknamed 'the lighthouse of the Pacific' — Captain Cook used its glow to navigate by at night in 1774, the first European record of the volcano.
puzzles.funFact: Captain Cook spotted Mount Yasur's glow from the sea in 1774 and used it to navigate by night — making it the first volcano in the Pacific to be recorded by a European explorer, over 250 years ago.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a city of 15 million where the call to prayer has echoed across seven hills for a thousand years
clues: Minarets and domes puncture a skyline stretching across seven hills above a famous strait — a city whose silhouette has defined the imagination of travellers since antiquity.
The call to prayer from hundreds of mosques echoes here across a metropolis of 15 million that has been capital of both the Roman and the Ottoman empires.
A covered bazaar here contains over 4,000 shops under one roof — in continuous operation since 1461 and receiving up to 400,000 visitors a day.
Its history spans three successive empires — Roman, Byzantine, and Ottoman — each leaving layers of architecture that coexist in the same streets and skyline.
Located in Turkey, this city straddles the Bosphorus strait — the only major city in the world where half sits in Europe and half in Asia, with millions crossing between continents daily.
puzzles.funFact: Istanbul is the only city in the world that sits on two continents — its European and Asian halves are connected by three suspension bridges and two undersea rail tunnels, with millions of people crossing between continents on their daily commute.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a city that reinvents itself completely every winter
clues: Each January, a flat field beside a frozen river is transformed into an illuminated city of palaces, pagodas, and cathedrals — every structure glowing from within against a −30°C sky.
Temperatures here regularly plunge below −30°C during construction, when thousands of workers spend weeks carving ice into architectural forms up to 50 metres tall.
The festival grew from a simple local tradition of ice lanterns into the world's largest snow and ice festival, attracting over a million visitors in a single season.
Located in Heilongjiang province in northeastern China near the Russian border, it draws blocks of ice cut directly from the frozen Songhua River.
The illuminated ice city covers over 600,000 square metres — roughly the same footprint as the entire principality of Monaco — built fresh from scratch every single year.
puzzles.funFact: The ice blocks used at Harbin are cut from the Songhua River in complete darkness at 3am, when the ice is thickest and clearest — each block is inspected for transparency before being hoisted by crane onto the building site.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to an island city where Arab, Persian, Indian, and African cultures fused into something entirely its own
clues: Carved wooden doors studded with brass spikes line the narrow streets of an old town where the architecture blends Islamic arches, Indian balconies, and Swahili craftsmanship.
The smell of cloves, cardamom, and coconut drifts through the alleyways — this island once supplied the world with the majority of its spice crop.
An Anglican cathedral stands directly over the site of the last open-air slave market in East Africa — a deliberate act of memorial where the altar stands where the whipping post once was.
Located on the island of Zanzibar off the coast of Tanzania, its historic centre is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and was once the capital of the Omani Sultanate.
Zanzibar Stone Town was the birthplace of Freddie Mercury — and the island is now famous worldwide both for its spice heritage and its white-sand beaches.
puzzles.funFact: Freddie Mercury was born in Zanzibar Stone Town in 1946 as Farrokh Bulsara — the island now has a dedicated museum in his honour, though he left as a child and spoke very little about his origins during his lifetime.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a volcanic island where female divers still harvest the sea floor by hand — some in their 80s
clues: A dormant shield volcano dominates the centre of an island whose lava tubes, black beaches, and tangerine orchards give it a landscape unlike anything else in its region.
The island is famous for its haenyeo — women divers, some in their 70s and 80s, who hold their breath and dive to the sea floor to harvest abalone and sea urchin by hand.
It has its own dialect incomprehensible to mainland speakers, its own UNESCO Intangible Heritage traditions, and its own set of creation myths involving giants who built the island.
Located off the southern tip of South Korea, it is the country's largest island and most popular domestic holiday destination, often called the 'Hawaii of Korea'.
Jeju Island's haenyeo — female free divers — are recognised by UNESCO as an Intangible Cultural Heritage. Some active divers are over 80 years old and dive to depths of 20 metres on a single breath.
puzzles.funFact: Because haenyeo women were the primary breadwinners in Jeju households for centuries, Jeju developed an unusually matriarchal social structure — men stayed home, raised children, and did housework while grandmothers dove to 20 metres to feed the family.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to one of the most desolate and dramatic coastlines on Earth — where the desert meets the fog and the ocean claims what it will
clues: A beach of black rock and rusted shipwrecks stretches into a grey murk so thick it erases the horizon — the ocean and the desert merge in eerie, impenetrable silence.
Hundreds of Cape fur seals haul themselves onto the shore, their barking audible from kilometres away, while jackals and brown hyenas patrol the colony edges.
Sailors who survived wrecks here rarely survived what came next — an unbroken desert with no freshwater for hundreds of kilometres in every direction.
Located along the northern coast of Namibia bordering Angola, it was named by the Bushmen 'The Land God Made in Anger' — and by Portuguese sailors 'The Gates of Hell'.
The Skeleton Coast gets its English name from the whale and seal bones that once blanketed the beach — and from the countless shipwrecks whose rusted hulks still protrude from the sand today.
puzzles.funFact: Over 1,000 ships have wrecked on the Skeleton Coast — the cold Benguela Current, dense fog, and violent surf made it one of the most dangerous stretches of ocean on Earth, and survivors who reached shore faced an unbroken desert with no water in any direction.
